name: Hair is law

lead: "Hair is law" is a slogan on looksmaxxing forums claiming that hair is the single most influential styling variable: the right cut or length frames the face, can make a jaw look stronger or a face shorter or rounder, and thick, healthy hair signals youth and health. Members use it to argue that fixing hair comes before more invasive changes.

Some members push back, arguing that hair is a disguise rather than a substitute for facial structure. Published research shows that hair thickness, shine and alignment change how women's hair is rated, while evidence on men's haircuts and face-shape matching is sparse.

paras: In forum guides, practitioners pick a haircut by face shape and head proportions, keep hair clean and conditioned, choose a length (the related slogan "long hair is law" favors longer styles), and treat thinning with approaches discussed elsewhere on the wiki. Barber visits and styling products are the usual tools.
Haircuts and grooming carry few risks. Related treatments for thinning hair, such as finasteride or minoxidil, have their own side-effect profiles covered on their own entries.

angle.text: Styling is applied immediately and is reversible, which is why forum guides place it early in an improvement routine. Proponents say a cut can imitate a stronger jawline or balance a long or round face.

lead: "Hair is law" (also written "hairlaw") is a maxim in looksmaxxing communities holding that hair outweighs many other features in how attractive a person looks. Proponents say a well-chosen style acts as a frame around the face: it can soften or sharpen features, lengthen or shorten the face's apparent shape, balance asymmetries and signal health.[1][2]

The phrase appears in forum megathreads and in offshoots such as "long hair is law," and it is usually framed as a first-line, reversible way to improve looks before pursuing surgery or other hardmaxxing routes, in the same softmaxxing tier as skincare, grooming and clothing.[1][3][4] Other members dispute the ranking, arguing that hair can only disguise a weak structure and that a face needs to be fixed first.[5]

Research supports a narrower version of the claim. Experiments with female wigs show that shine, alignment and volume shift ratings of age, health and attractiveness.[6] Studies of men's head hair and haircuts matched to face shape are limited; the better-studied male variables are facial hair and hair loss, where results differ between studies.[7][8]
infobox: Haircut, hair length, hair health, hair loss
Hair is among the most influential visual variables
Women's hair shine and alignment [6]; men's facial hair [7]
Finasteride, minoxidil, hair transplantation for hair loss [8]

paras: A forum guide titled "Hair is law" opens by calling men's hair a strategic tool for social projection and a "visual frame" for the face, saying a cut can simulate a better jawline, shorten a very long face or lengthen a round one.[1][2] It lists perception of symmetry, projection of health and modulation of facial shape as the main mechanisms, and says thick, clean hair is associated with health and favorable genetics.[1]
The guide's author reported problems uploading images and posted it in a second thread; replies were mostly appreciative.[2]

Wikipedia describes looksmaxxing as an online practice, coined on incel message boards in the 2010s and popularised on TikTok in the 2020s, that ranges from skincare and gym use (softmaxxing) to surgery and drugs (hardmaxxing). It notes that men's magazines such as GQ, Esquire and Men's Health long promoted similar skincare and hairstyle advice.[4] Hair is a softmaxxing topic: cheap, quickly changed and reversible, which is the logic behind placing it first in improvement routines.

Hair also links to other entries on the wiki. Thinning hair is discussed alongside finasteride, minoxidil and transplants, and beards are discussed as a way of altering the lower face, as in the forum remark that a beard can make a weak chin look strong.[5]

Proponents' strongest version is that hair can "fix" what surgery otherwise would. One forum reply states the logic as: if something cannot be fixed, it can be disguised, comparing a weak chin hidden by a beard to its appearance when shaved.[5]
Skeptical members argue the opposite order. A thread titled for women at the poster's school valuing hair above all argues that the face should be addressed before covering it with long hair.[5]
The slogan has variants, for example "long hair is law," which promotes length specifically.[3]

Wikipedia's history of long hair on men shows how much its reception has varied. Long hair signalled wealth in ancient Greece, short hair marked servitude in parts of the Middle Ages, the Beatles popularised long male hair in the 1960s and it peaked in the 1960s and 1970s, with mockery in the 1980s and later revival, including the 'man bun'.[9] The same article says its attractiveness research concerns women's hair, not men's.[9]

Wikipedia's article on hairstyles notes that hairstyles signal class, age and attitudes, that natural hair is linked to perceived health, and that men's styles in Western societies have tended to be more uniform than women's.[10] The article on physical attractiveness lists hair texture among the pillars of beauty proposed by Grammer and colleagues, alongside youthfulness, symmetry and skin complexion.[11] These sources describe hair as one cue among several, not a ranked first.

A 2025 study in the International Journal of Cosmetic Science had women in Germany, Spain and the USA rate wigs on a model. High-shine hair was rated younger, healthier and more attractive than low-shine hair in all three countries (500 raters each), and in a second experiment with 2,000 US women, straight-aligned hair was rated most youthful, healthy and attractive regardless of colour or head angle, with shine a weaker factor.[6] The authors said the effects remained visible in small, phone-sized images.[6]
Earlier work reported by Wikipedia found that women's hair length and quality correlated with age and perceived health (Hinsz, Matz and Patience, 2001).[9] These studies concern female hair.

For men, the research is mainly about facial hair. A feature in The Psychologist's research digest summarises studies with differing results: bearded men rated more attractive in a 1973 study and in a 2016 Archives of Sexual Behavior study, clean-shaven men rated younger and more attractive in a 1991 study, and a further 2016 paper finding no main effect of facial hair growth on attractiveness; a cross-cultural study found beards raised ratings of age and status but not attractiveness.[7] One study suggested beards boosted attractiveness when they made a man stand out among clean-shaven faces.[7]

Hair loss is the other studied variable. Wikipedia reports that pattern hair loss is a moderately stressful condition that reduces body-image satisfaction for many men, that a 2001 South Korean study found balding men rated less attractive, while a 2002 Welsh survey found women rated bald and grey-haired men as quite desirable.[8] It lists styling, shaving the head and scalp tattoos as camouflage and finasteride, minoxidil and transplantation as treatments.[8] Little peer-reviewed work tests whether matching a haircut to face shape changes ratings.

No studies found on the "hair is law" claim itself. Related experimental research on hair shine, alignment and perceived attractiveness exists for women's hair,[6] and research on facial hair and on hair loss exists for men.[7][8]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the phrase is used both as a rallying cry and as a target of disagreement, usually in threads about haircuts and hair care.[1][5]

Longer hair is better ("long hair is law")

timeline.event: Long male hair signals wealth and power; many Greek men move to shorter styles around the 6th century BC.[9]
Louis XIII of France is said to pioneer the male wig after beginning to go bald.[10]
The Beatles popularise long male hair; it becomes a countercultural marker.[9]
A study reports bearded men judged better-looking by undergraduates.[7]
Hinsz, Matz and Patience report that women's hair length and quality correlate with age and perceived health.[9]
Looksmaxxing terms emerge on incel and manosphere message boards.[4]
Looksmaxxing spreads on TikTok; forum guides such as the "Hair is law" megathread circulate.[4][2]
International Journal of Cosmetic Science publishes wig experiments on shine and alignment with raters in three countries.[6]
